title: Ambedkar's vows
hookLine: his twenty-two vows, and a Buddhism centered on equality

cards: After the refuges, Ambedkar didn't step down. The crowd was still standing on the open ground in Nagpur. He read out a list of vows, twenty-two of them, and asked them to take every one with him, line by line.

Some sound like what anyone taking refuge might promise: keep the precepts, follow the eightfold path. Others are sharp, and meant to be. Running through the whole list, like a spine, is one idea: every person is equal.

teach.b: First, the vows that turn away. A number of them ask his followers to leave behind the gods, rites and caste customs of the faith they were born into.
Those vows were written for his own followers, out of his history and theirs, and Hindu readers may see them very differently. This lesson simply says what they say, and judges no one.
Second, the vows that turn toward. Others commit to the Buddha's teaching: to keep the precepts, not to kill, steal or lie, to practice compassion and loving-kindness, and to walk the eightfold path.
These would sound familiar in a monastery in Burma or Thailand. Third, rivers into the ocean. Among the vows is a plain statement that all people are equal, and a promise to work to make that true.
An old picture in the Pali texts fits it.
The Buddha compares the great rivers that flow into the ocean and lose their names there to people of every caste who join his order: once inside, the old names no longer count.
Ambedkar read the Buddha's community in that spirit, as a place where caste dissolves. Fourth, a Buddhism for now.
His followers sometimes call this reading Navayana, a new vehicle: the Buddha's path as freedom inside the mind and also freedom in society.
Some Buddhists of other schools question parts of his reinterpretation; his followers hear in it the Buddha speaking straight into their lives.
Either way, in these vows equality isn't only a feeling. It's a promise you say out loud.

how: At conversion ceremonies in the Ambedkarite tradition, new Buddhists take the three refuges and the five precepts and then recite Ambedkar's twenty-two vows together.

practice: Bring to mind three people: someone you look up to, someone you barely notice, and someone you find hard.

See each as a river with its own name, running toward the same wide sea, and with each out-breath let the names soften until all three rest level in the water. You don't have to like them all; just see them as equal for a moment.
